clinicalPearls: Presents with sudden, painless loss of a sector of the visual field corresponding to the territory of the occluded arteriole
The fundus shows cloudy white inner retinal oedema confined to the affected sector, with narrowed arterioles and segmented (boxcar) blood flow
A visible embolus may be seen lodged at an arteriolar bifurcation, most often a refractile cholesterol (Hollenhorst) plaque, or a calcific or platelet-fibrin embolus
Carotid atheroma is the commonest embolic source, followed by cardiac sources such as valvular disease and atrial fibrillation
In older patients giant cell arteritis must be excluded urgently, as it can cause arteritic occlusion and threaten the fellow eye
A retinal arterial occlusion is regarded as a stroke equivalent and mandates prompt systemic vascular assessment
There is no proven sight-restoring ocular therapy, so management focuses on identifying and treating the embolic source and reducing future vascular risk
reference.pathophysiology: An embolus becomes impacted at a retinal arteriolar bifurcation, acutely interrupting perfusion of the downstream retina. The inner retinal layers, supplied by the retinal circulation, undergo ischaemic infarction that appears as cloudy white opacification of the affected sector. Emboli are typically cholesterol fragments from carotid atheroma, calcific material from cardiac valves, or platelet-fibrin aggregates. In arteritic cases, giant cell arteritis causes inflammatory occlusion of the arterial supply rather than embolism.
additionalDifferentials: Cotton-wool spot from another retinal vascular disorder
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to define the ischaemic sector and search for an embolus
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein to screen for giant cell arteritis
Carotid Doppler ultrasound to identify a stenosing or ulcerated plaque
Cardiac evaluation including electrocardiography and echocardiography for an embolic source
Fluorescein angiography showing delayed arteriolar filling in the affected territory
Blood pressure, glucose and lipid assessment for vascular risk factors
redFlags: Symptoms of giant cell arteritis such as headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness, requiring urgent corticosteroids
Concurrent neurological symptoms suggesting cerebral infarction
Multiple or bilateral emboli suggesting a major cardiac or aortic source
Occlusion in a young patient, prompting a search for a cardiac or thrombophilic cause
reference.prognosis: The corresponding visual field defect is usually permanent, although central acuity is often preserved when the fovea is spared; the greater concern is the elevated risk of subsequent stroke or other systemic vascular events.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude giant cell arteritis in an older patient
Not referring urgently for stroke and cardiovascular workup
Mistaking sectoral arterial whitening for a branch vein occlusion
Reassuring the patient without pursuing the embolic source
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
